title: Confronting the Governance Gap: How AI Is Outpacing Enterprise Oversight
author: Tonie Marie Gordon, PhD
summary: Tonie Marie Gordon argues that enterprise AI governance fails not for lack of policy but because practice departs from policy under pressure. She cites an EY survey in which 98% of large companies have formal AI governance yet 47% set it aside for urgent deployments, and a PwC study in which 93% call oversight critical but only 7% have it consistently embedded. Drawing on Meyer and Rowan's idea of formal structure as ceremony, she says governance becomes a legitimacy ritual decoupled from the work it governs. Autonomous agents sharpen the problem because they pass a pre-deployment approval gate once and then act continuously beyond it. She identifies three weak points: missing inventories of agents, override authority without the competence to use it, and accountability that sits with technology rather than the business. She closes with five tests of oversight integrity covering exceptions, inventory, runtime oversight, competence and ownership that leaders can apply to any agentic deployment.
points: The central gap is behavioral and institutional: nearly every large firm has an AI policy, but nearly half bypass it when deployments are urgent.
Agentic systems defeat gate-based governance because oversight happens once before launch while the agent keeps acting for months afterward.
Oversight needs visibility and competence, and the survey data show many firms cannot detect unauthorized agents and are unsure staff understand AI's limits.
Accountability is misplaced when the technology function owns AI-supported decisions whose consequences fall on the business.
The five tests (exception, inventory, runtime, competence, ownership) give leaders concrete questions and controls, such as logging every exception and naming a business owner for each agent.
quotes: The policy exists, but the practice departs from it under pressure. That pressure is intensifying as organizations hand consequential actions to autonomous agents that operate faster than any review cycle built for human decisions.
A governance policy held by 98% of firms and set aside by nearly half of them for urgent deployments fits this pattern closely. The urgency exception is the mechanism for the decoupling.
The 26% of agentic adopters unable to detect unauthorized agents face a problem no review protocol can solve, because their governance process cannot know which systems it’s responsible for.
an organization can hold the authority to intervene without the competence to know when intervention is warranted.
This arrangement separates the people who oversee a system from the people who bear its outcomes, which weakens oversight as a check.
A rising exception rate is a leading indicator and deserves the same attention as a rising incident rate.
An approval granted before launch says little about an agent’s behavior in its sixth month of operation.
